utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T. The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we start hearing the evidence of the next witness, I have a few matters I would like to raise with you. The first one, there has been some discussion about how to deal with the 54 bis hearing. The Chamber suggests the following: If we have heard the representatives of the Republic of Serbia that if that raises any matter of concern or whether -- if you'd like to make any observation, that it be done immediately during that hearing for both parties, which gives an opportunity also that if that, again, raises issues on which we'd like to hear further from Serbia that we could do that right away, rather than asking for written submissions and then giving the opportunity to the Republic of Serbia to respond to that. It may take quite a while. I think the issues are fairly clear and that so, therefore, the Chamber a suggested that we proceed in that way. Any comments? Not from you, not from you. Then, perhaps, meanwhile, the witness could already be brought into the courtroom. The Chamber has decided on the 92 bis submissions for some other witnesses. You'll get these decisions but I already hereby informed the Stanisic Defence that the Chamber requires the presence of witness DST-071 for cross-examination. So this part of the motion for 92 bis is denied and if you call him then he will be a 92 ter witness. And we'd very much like to know when you intend to call this witness, preferably by this Friday, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We'll do our best. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the hearing of Thursday, the 1st of December, is cancelled. But this hearing is moved to the afternoon of the Monday before, that's the 28th of November, so we'll sit in that week on Monday instead of Thursday. I know, Mr. Petrovic, that this is the first week in which you call witnesses, so be prepared that we start on Monday afternoon already and not on Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the hearing of Tuesday, the 29th of November is moved from the afternoon to the morning, so we'll sit Monday afternoon; Tuesday morning; Wednesday morning, most likely 15 bis; and not on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can hear me in a language you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have been informed that you would prefer to give your testimony in English language rather than to speak Dutch and through an interpreter. We, perhaps, would not need an interpreter but that's your preference, is that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For your colleagues it's probably better to do it in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Well, we could have done it through an interpreter. If you at any point in time have any problem with mastering of the English language, then please let me know, I'll not serve as an interpreter but we'll find a solution for it. Then before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but truth. The text is handed out to you now, would you please stand and make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Helgers, because we were informed that you are Mr. Helgers. But that may be the first question that Mr. Jordash will put to you. Mr. Jordash is counsel for the Defence and he will first -- counsel for the Defence of Mr. Stanisic, and he will be the first one to examine you. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Helgers?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As perhaps is plain, we haven't met. I want to go through some formalities before we proceed with the examination. First of all, were you provided with a copy of --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me have on the screen, please, 1D03910.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Were you provided with a statement dated the 3rd of August, 1995, which purported to be a statement by you, were you provided that this morning upon your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I don't see any picture, but I did receive this morning statements dated at or about the 3rd of August of 1995, as well of a transcript of my statement in the trial against Mr. Karadzic in January this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, let me just deal first of all with the statement that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That would be my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's your signature at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And did you look through the statement and confirm it's a statement that you gave?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, and with regards to the statement, during the trial against Mr. Karadzic I made two very small notes about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Which we'll see reflected in a transcript which we'll look at in a moment?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Apart from those amendments having reviewed it again today, was there anything else you would like to amend?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And were the contents of that statement in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: They are in accordance with the truth and I remember them or I should say as I remember them at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And if asked the same questions concerning the events, you'd answer in substance the same way?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you answer, in substance, the same way if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Probably not literally, but in substance, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender that as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D510, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I saw on the chart that there are no objections against admission of the statement of Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing there, then D510 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And could we have on the screen, please, 1D03909.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the transcript I take it, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is, if I'm well informed, not on the 65 ter list, but may I take it that you want when you tender it that you also ask it to be admitted to the 65 ter -- added to the 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it there are no objections against that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm told it is on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'm wrongly informed. Apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to review this transcript, the evidence you gave in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And, again, do you have any clarifications or amendments to make to that transcript?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Apart from some name errors and the continued reference to radio station instead of radar station, I think in essence it's the correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you be able it to indicate the corrections you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, several times there have been mentioned radio station as the location to which I was transferred, and I kept hostage. And that's radar station. And as I remember I said or at least I intended to say radar station and not a radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps I can deal with this globally, is that the radar station at Jahorina?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: So where there's reference in the statement to radio station at Jahorina, and you being held at that location, it in fact should read radar station?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. And sorry, your second amendment was?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Some names that were spelled phonetically and not always correctly, but, okay, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can you think of any now?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Mr. Raamakers is spelled several times differently, but okay, that's minor issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But the names themselves that you wish to correct, phonetically they read as ...?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Raamakers, well the same name is spelled two times differently phonetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know how to should be spelled?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Phonetically.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, actually?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: R-a-a-m-a-k-e-r-s.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you think of any others?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: It's being spelled -- yes, that's correct. Not at the moment, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If at any stage you think of any, please indicate.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: There might be some very minor details, but, I mean, they will be minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this as an exhibit, please, Your Honour. Perhaps I should ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was what you said there in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Of course. As I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you would give the same answers if asked the same questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, the number would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number for document 1D3909 would be D511, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at the parties, no objections. D511 is admitted into evidence and prior to admitting it leave has been granted to add it to the 65 ter list. No, it was on the 65 ter list. My apologies. Yes, for the second time. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now if I may -- or perhaps one last thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we perhaps on the screen -- could I just have a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where I earlier made a mistake I think it was about the associated exhibits; they were not all on the 65 ter list, I think. I don't know whether you want to address that. Either now or at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If I may do that later. We've been in discussions with the Prosecution, so there's agreement on many of them, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I want to move fairly swiftly and have you look at some documents, if I may, Mr. Helgers, and ask you to testify to some of the contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05156, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: As you'll appreciate, we don't need to go through your testimony and repeat what is in your statement or transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, if you could tell us where we find the document on the chart, it makes it easier for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the top of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it, yes, number 30. Or am I wrong? 1D0 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you working from the Prosecution chart?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm working from the chart in which we read whether there are any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could you take a moment just to read through that document, please, Mr. Helgers?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Could it be enlarged just a little bit. Thank you. Can you please continue scrolling, thank you. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And the next page so you get a full picture of the contents of this, please.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page, are you able to shed any light on this what document is, where it emanates from? Do you recognise the format?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: It seems to be quite in accordance with the type of format we used to report events.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We being?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: UNMOs. Although, it did not originate from my team.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Right. And do you confirm or are you able to shed any light on the comment there on the first page about when the first attack took place, which is, I think the third paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Yes, I remember that it was stated and we were informed that there had been an air-strike the day before we were taken hostage. Was on 25 of May. And allegedly, as far as I remember, the -- it was in response to the non-compliance of the Bosnian Serb armed forces with an order, if you could say so, to withdraw a number of artillery, heavy weapons, I should say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In relation to this report, this is the 25th of May, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- do you know if those artillery, heavy weapons were withdrawn at any stage?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: As I recall, although of course I was not present at the withdrawal or not, they were not withdrawn or not withdrawn entirely. That was the impression I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the third paragraph starting with: [As read] "This attack was in response to the UN's claim that the Serb side did not return for artillery pieces into WCPs but although Muslim artillery remains positioned inside the Sarajevo exclusion zones, only Serb targets were bombed. Muslims were even firing today on the Serb parts of Sarajevo with mortars and Brownings." Just immediately before the 25th of May, were there bombings from both sides of the, as I say, ethnic divide?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Which exact time do you refer?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, the days running up to the bombings by NATO and also your detention?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Okay. From the area where we were stationed we could formally see almost every day a few grenades being lobbed into Sarajevo proper, which is the Bosniak-held Sarajevo. I do remember that several times there were also incoming shells, yes, that means that there were shelling from probably presumably the Bosniak-held areas into Serb-held areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At number 2, just further down on this first page, there's a number of complaints being registered concerning the perceived lack of neutrality of NATO. Did you ever hear those complaints before or during or after your detention?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From which kind of people?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I was aware that the Bosnian Serbs had, in general, the opinion that they were more often targeted and as reason for our detention was given several times by several different persons that it was to -- in response to the attacks of the NATO against Bosnian Serbs targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: When you say Bosnian Serbs, are we talking about the military or civilians or both?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: As far as I am -- I know, the military, but there were reports by Bosnian Serbs TV and radio, presumably, I was told that were also civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In terms of -- if we look at page 2 of this document, for example, there's a report at the last paragraph about: [As read] "As far as the locals see it, UN is once again singling out the Serbs for blame. They cannot understand why the Muslims go unpunished for the shelling and shooting that they inflict on Serb civilians in and around Sarajevo ...," and so on. Are you able to comment on the locals view on what was happening?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Due to the restriction of movement my contact with locals was fairly limited. However, I do notice that, in general, Bosnian Serb press, especially TV, was very much giving attention to the supposed unfair treatment of the UN and of NATO against the Bosnian Serbs. But of course, as I told you, that's what I got via our translators from the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was there any perception prior to your detention or during your detention that there may be any reaction by the locals to your presence on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I can only say that up until shortly before our detention the contacts I had, which were limited as I told you before, were quite correct. I never experienced any -- well, we were not very welcome, but I did not perceive any real hostility against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And after the air-strikes began?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, the situation deteriorated a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In what sense? Can you be a bit more concrete, please?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: As probably, as I'm sure has been said in my statement of August 1995, and also in my transcripts, after the air-strikes on the 26th, we got a visit from, I think it was the deputy battalion commander, first, of the local battalion, Bosnian Serb battalion about the air-strike and he was quite -- he was not happy, let me put it like that. Later on, I think it was the security chief, he came back and he was quite negative and he gave us basically house arrest and told us that if we were going outside, we would be shot. That was mainly the -- so that was Bosnian Serb military response which was obviously quite negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Was he suggesting you were going to be shot by the Bosnian Serb military or by civilians with arms, what was the understanding you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: As I recall, he said if you go outside, you will be shot. He did not state by whom. At least not to my recollection, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we have on the screen, please, 1D05161. And it's -- it's at 34, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt. For my objection can I have private session, please, for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We move into private session. For the public gallery, that also means that the curtain has to be down for a second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And could the curtains be open as soon as reasonably possible. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If you just have a quick look at the document on the screen, again dated the 25th of May, which is the day before your arrest or detention, I should say. And there's a report there on the radio, it says from Banja Luka Northern Bosnia with Karadzic saying: "If (UN Bosnian commander Lieutenant-General Rupert) Smith orders air-strikes against us, we will treat them (the United Nations) as enemies." Is that something that you heard at the time or became aware of later?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I do remember that shortly before we were taken hostage, and I think it was the evening of the 25th, the situation was considered to be worsening, security situation and in fact, I do record that our deputy team leader at the moment, Major Westlund, he tried to get the mission to withdraw to the local UN Battalion, which was not approved. So our understanding as the team was that the situation was deteriorating, the security situation. I don't recall this exact statement, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have please, video 1D05270 at 20.48 please we'll play it to 21.47.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I stop it a moment, please. There is a translation and I thought it had be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the transcript provided to the booth? I see nodding no from the booth.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Perhaps it could be provided now, please. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, your estimate was 30 minutes, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I had in my mind it was 45 minutes, but since Your Honours just said that, I think you are right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I shall cut matters short very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus very much on what is in dispute and what is not in dispute. I mean, that there may have been different views at the time as to the justification of the air-strikes, but that seems at least not to be the core of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes. Could we please play this video.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Our lives are in danger too. The NATO bombed Serbian civilian targets, did you have any problems with Serbian soldiers? Answer: No, not at the moment, we don't have, we did not have any problem at the moment. And you are from? I'm from Spain. So this is how UNPROFOR members were situated in one of the bridges. They are placed at all key positions where NATO could bomb again and we will visit some of them."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recognise anybody in the video?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, the first person speaking seems to be, again, he is a colleague. I don't remember his name but I met him just before our release.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And -- what this video depicts, was this representative of where you and other hostages were held, the type of locations?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: They seem to -- this seemed to be held at the bridge, so I was held at a radar station.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: What about other hostages?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I know from some who had been held, one Dutch colleague at least, near a aircraft shelter in Banja Luka and others were kept near bridges and other locations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there any dispute about these kind of matters reading the statement, not, are you going to dispute the places where people were chained to --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, therefore it seems not to be very much in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me move forward to the time of your release. You were - is this right? - released on the 18th of June, and at that point, according to your statement, Koljevic made a speech to you?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were then spoken to by Colonel Indjic?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Lieutenant-colonel in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, yes. And then at some point taken by bus to the Presidency in Pale and at that point you had a meeting with the security chief of Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just so we are clear, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: To be quite honest, he was introduced to me as the security chief of Mr. Milosevic. At that time I, well, being very relieved at our pending release, I must say I don't recall the name at that moment. I do remember him entering the bus where all the -- the last batch of hostages was in at the moment and him stating that he was security chief of Mr. Milosevic and that Mr. Milosevic had arranged for our release.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall anything else that was said by the security chief?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Anything specifically?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, if you recall anything else specifically?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I remember he said -- I think he said the good offices, but of course it was translated because my Serbo-Croatian or Croatian or Serbian is not so good. Through the good offices of Mr. Milosevic, that's what I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. And he asked if you wanted to speak to the press?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Ah yes, I do remember that. And we spoke to each other, we didn't really want to and after they insisted, I think it was Captain Rechner, of the Canadian armed forces, also an UNMO previously stationed in Pale, went outside and a short statement to the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you recall what he said?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: It was outside so obviously not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Can I have on the screen and play 1D05254. In fact, we can probably deal with it by transcript only. 1D05254.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we have to play it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, the transcript is sufficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have any specific questions you can put them to the witness. Ms. Marcus, it is undisputed that these were the words spoken by Mr. Stanisic at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I just ask you something. Did you ever learn the name of the security chief?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, later.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And it was?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: When I was contacted by, in fact, Mr. Knoops, when he asked me if I wanted to act as a witness for the Defence. I probably -- very probably, I've heard the name before, but it didn't linger in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. Were these words then, was anything else said?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: It was -- at least not as it was translated to us, in my recollection. I think, I do seem to remember that Captain Rechner translated but he translated quite shortly, not literally, and I do remember that the last part that we were handed over to the security force of the Serb Republic and that we were going to be brought to Serbia, to Yugoslavia, I should say, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This could create some confusion, let's clarify with the witness. When you said the Serb Republic, you were not referring to Republika Srpska but you were referring to the republic of at that moment still was the Republic of Serbia, being part of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are completely correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I have, please, on the screen, 1D05158. Which is at number 32, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a report by the medical doctors of the Keran [phoen] VB military hospital regarding a visit to UN officers prisoners at the Keran barracks?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any disputes about the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see on the table that the Prosecution no objection if tendered from the bar table, if they would consider it unreliable, then I take it there would have been some objection. Ms. Marcus, any dispute.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then I won't show you that document, Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you want to tender it from the bar table as confirmation of the medical state in which -- of the hostages.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or at least the persons that were released. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number would be D513.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And in that document, Mr. Helgers, you may be the only detainee there that wasn't suffering from any problems during detention but we know from your transcript later on that you did suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do you know if others suffered from such problems later on?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I'd rather not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, if you know, you should answer that question, however, if you want to protect the privacy of former colleagues then we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm not interested in their names, just a general view of what the impact of this detention on the hostages in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you know, tell us, if not, please tell us as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know of several colleagues who later got problems, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Problems similar to yours, is that how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Similars to yours, I'm not a doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to mine, but to yours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't comment if it was post-traumatic stress or something similar, but let's say problems related to their experiences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean psychological problems related to that experience?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Finally then, then I'll sit down, how did the security chief treat you and the remaining hostages? Can you remember his approach to you?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, as I told you, he came into the bus and he made a statement which was not literally, but was more or less translated by Captain Rechner, and afterwards, I can't really comment on himself, but I can comment on the Yugoslav security forces, they were correct. Although, I should say we -- I at least, and I think most of my colleagues were not in the mood to be very friendly or talkative with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Understandable. I can show you a document, but there's a document here which is D00475 MFI, an exhibit in this trial, which has the number of hostages at the total number at 441. Is that something that you are able to comment on?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I remember that initially I was told that there were several hundreds. I think something like 400 were named hostages. Especially from the battalions, from the troop fighters. And UNMOs, the number of UNMOs was considerably smaller, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Nothing further. Thank you, Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jordash. Mr. Petrovic, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no questions. Not for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions. Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. Ms. Marcus, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll now be cross-examined by Ms. Marcus, Ms. Marcus is counsel for the Prosecution Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, thank you for your willingness to come and answer our questions. I am going to ask you a few questions about the media coverage during the release. Do you recall the media coverage between the trip, during the trip from Pale to Novi Sad when you went by bus, do you recall any media coverage during that trip?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: There was quite a lot of media coverage. I don't know exactly which events you mean specifically. There was a lot of media coverage during our release at -- as we were -- before we were put in the bus. Then there was, well, a tremendous media coverage, I think it was from international press near the residency of the house of Mr. Karadzic, and then there was a third media event, I'm forgetting the exact location, at the bridge was the border between the Bosnian Serb area and Serbia or former Yugoslavia, and then when we were -- when we stepped out of the bus, I think it was in Novi Sad, at the hotel, there was another big media event.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During the process of these media events, were you informed of what was going on? Were you kept informed of why the buses were stopping, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not specifically. I mean, it was obvious that it was for media coverage, all the photos were being taken from the bus and from several times we were asked to give interviews or somebody came to the bus to ask if we wanted to give interviews. Not specifically why we were stopping at a specific place, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, I would have the same question, to what extent is there dispute about media coverage on the events?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm finished with this subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you would say, I would have asked this question before you started the subject, you -- I'm looking at the material, I'd very much like the parties to focus on the issue at stake and if I understand the Defence well, that there was some emphasis on the event itself and there seems not to be much dispute about that, and then mainly the role of Mr. Stanisic in releasing the hostages, Mr. Jordash, if I'm correctly -- if I understand your position correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, I think, we should focus on that. It's not your witness, Ms. Marcus, you'll cross-examine the witness on this matter. And the hostage matter itself is not directly part of your case, is it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I then, rather than showing the witness, tender one more clip of one press conference into evidence. I think this is then not going to be disputed in my view. It's uploaded as 65 ter 4755.2. It is another clip from exhibit P49 already admitted. There were four clips admitted from that, this is one more clip, it's a press conference that I believe took place in Novi Sad. I'm seeking to tender it from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I haven't yet seen it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps, how long is it? Ms. Marcus, you said it was ...? If it's a short clip.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Approximately one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's play it. That takes less time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "This time I particularly refer also to the efforts of the new French government because those who wished to return to their battalions, the 26. Besides in this agreement, the Muslim side did not facilitate the return to their battalions for the last 15 observers who are still detained. The detainees will be released by the end of the week. Ladies and gentlemen, last time when we have our government ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The question I was going to ask the witness, Your Honour, is just one question, whether you recall being present during this particular press conference?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can it be tendered from the bar table, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't understand the relevance or the probative value of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus. The witness cannot tell us anything about it, but what is the relevance of ...

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'll withdraw it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Major Helgers, I'm going to now ask you a few questions step by step through the release process. I'm going to ask you about some of your observations and how you felt. Firstly, can you tell us -- you've told us about some of the longer term repercussions of your experience. Can you tell us in just a few words how you felt during the time that you were detained, specifically, how you felt with respect to your Bosnian Serb captors?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: When I was leaving the radar station, I remember commenting to some of them that I would be seeing them here in The Hague in the future, which implies that I was -- although they at the radar station generally treated us correctly, I was not very well -- very positively inclined towards them.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Can you describe to the best of your recollection when was the first moment you realised that you might be released?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's a bit of a difficult question. I remember after one week, exactly one week on the Friday, we by radio, BBC World, we received information that some of the UN hostages were being released however there was an incident with the shooting down of an American airplane and the situation deteriorated again for some time. And then, step by step, they were releasing slowly several of the UN personnel so we were in good hopes that we would be released eventually.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you remember where you were when you first had that hope, that you would be released?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Marcus, I have to really raise a matter. This witness has been called by the Stanisic Defence, I take it to confirm the role of Mr. Stanisic in the release. If there's any dispute about this role, that is certainly a matter which should be raised also in cross-examination. In his examination-in-chief, Mr. Jordash already hinted at that it's not pleasant to be a hostage and I think there's no dispute about that, is there? Because the questions you are asking, how did you feel, of course everyone feels very badly, I would say it's almost a notorious fact, if you are kept hostage it doesn't feel good. If there's any hope that you will be released, does that feel better? Well, I would say you may have some doubts as to whether it would happen or not but apart from whether there's notorious fact, I don't think there's much dispute about that, is there, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Let's try to focus on why this witness is here, not to tell us that it was bad because that's not in dispute and I have -- I may have some compassion with a witness who comes and has to tell about these things because it must have been a very bad experience. No doubt about that, but for this case, this being -- not being disputed, and in view of the obvious reason why the Stanisic Defence has called this witness, there seems to be not much reason to go into these areas. Would you please keep that in your mind. And also whether it was right or wrong, there I was about to stop Mr. Jordash whether there were good excuses for behaving in this way or whether there were good -- well, not only to behave in this way but why you could be emotional and do, perhaps, things wrongly which you shouldn't have done but that the circumstances make it very explainable that you would do that, that's all not, I think, what the witness is here for. Mr. Helgers, don't gain the impression that you are here for nothing, not at all. We've carefully read your statement and your testimony and, Ms. Marcus, could you please keep it in mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, thank you very much for your intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, I'm trying to find out from you if you can tell me when did you first come to understand that it was the Serb authorities from Serbia who were going to be involved in your release?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I was told it by the security chief of Mr. Milosevic obviously. However, before -- I don't know exactly where, but I was under the impression, I got the impression that there were negotiations going on and including obviously Mr. Milosevic because it was well known that he had very cosy relationship with Mr. Karadzic and his government.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: In your ICTY statement you say, this is referring to -- sorry, this is referring to Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic, and you say: "He signed a document and some guy from Serb security forces with a red beret signed a document and we were handed over."

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Could I ask you about this person from the Serb security forces with the red beret. Now, first, this was before you were addressed by the security chief of Milosevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That is correct. However, I should say that I got the information that it was a Serb security officer from comments made by other UNMOs. We were not personally really very well informed by either the Bosnian Serb forces or the Serb forces about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall seeing that individual arrive?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I don't recall. He must have arrived obviously, but not really.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you informed of what his identity was? Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I don't have any recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And do you recall if he was accompanied by anyone?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I think there was -- there was obviously apart from Bosnian Serb press there were some other officials. I think Mr. Koljevic was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, if I'm not mistaken, this signing of the document for your release happened before the press conference at the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct it was the handing over, I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The handing over. Can you tell me where that took place physically?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That was at a, I think it was a barracks. No, it was -- Jesus, I seem to be having a blackout.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. But it wasn't at the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No, definitely at the Presidency. It was at the place where we were loaded later on in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And that is where you were -- from there you were taken to the Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: We were held at the barracks. From the barracks we were brought to this location, I think it was a hospital, but I'm not quite sure. There the -- there was that ceremony, that was the Bosnian Serb press very present, making -- making tapes obviously. And after signing or some ceremony in Serb, of which I didn't understand a lot obviously, we were taken to -- we were put in the bus and brought to the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. Just before you were taken to the Presidency, when you saw that individual from the Serbian state security arrive, were you able to observe any interaction between that individual and your Bosnian Serb captors?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, they were. They were talking of course, obviously. And for us, I mean, we knew we were being collected to be released quickly so although I didn't understand exactly what was happening, I could deduce it.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Who was it who took you from that location where the release document was signed to the Presidency in Pale, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I have no recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So would you say that the hand-over took place right there after the document was signed, or would you say the hand-over to the Serbian authorities took place sometime later, in your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I can't exactly recollect that and that's because, for me, the real release was when I arrived in Zagreb a day later. To be quite honest, I did not feel very much released in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I understand. I hope you'll bear with me for a few more details and anything you remember is fine, anything you don't, of course you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one clarifying question. You said you only felt relief "when I was in Zagreb, I did not feel released in the former Yugoslavia." That Zagreb is as far as I know the former Yugoslavia, so but the -- you wanted to refer to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia I think comprising of Serbia, including Kosovo obviously, and Montenegro, if I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that they exchanged greetings, in other words the officials who had come from Serbia exchanged greeting with the Bosnian Serbs, do you recall them exchanging salutes of any kind?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not specifically. I think there were but I'm -- I couldn't swear to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at the Presidency building, trying to draw your attention to outside the building before you entered. Do you recall observing who was present outside, vehicles, forces, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, lots of vehicles, lots of press obviously, and also several persons wearing the, I think it was red or reddish berets of the Serb -- the former Yugoslavia, Yugoslavian Republic of Yugoslavia, of Milosevic Yugoslavia, his forces, the Red Berets and several police cars, et cetera, et cetera. It was quite a cavalcade going to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say police cars, are you referring to police cars from Serbia or local Bosnian Serb police cars, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I don't recall. I think there were military, I think the Serbian security forces, they had their own cars but there were also some Bosnian Serb police cars in my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, you may have partially answered this already but how were the forces from Serbia distinguishable to you from the local forces?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: By the red berets and the fact they were pointed out to me as being the Yugoslav security forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall if they were armed?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I think they were armed, but I am -- I couldn't swear to that. I probably would have noted if they hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, entering the Presidency in Pale, do you recall who escorted you in? In other words, which forces escorted you in?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: To be -- to be specific, we didn't enter the Presidency, the bus was taken to in front of the Presidency and I think it was a combination of the Yugoslav forces because we were handed over there and some local forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: When you say you didn't enter the Presidency, you never entered the Presidency during the process?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: What happened, the bus was brought from our -- from where the hand-over ceremony was to in front of the Presidency where there was a big media event which is what I remember most, and the speech of the security chief of Mr. Milosevic. We did not enter the building. We stayed in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: So where -- I'm just trying to understand because when we observe the video of the press conference where Mr. Stanisic introduces himself as the security chief of Mr. Milosevic, this appears to be indoors. So I'm just trying to understand if there was a separate address to you or if it was the press conference that you viewed?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No, what I remember of the security chief of Mr. Milosevic, is that he entered the bus and that he -- he -- that he stated that Mr. Milosevic had arranged for our release, as I stated earlier. I did not enter the building. I did not leave the bus at that moment. I think the only one who left the bus at that moment was, in my recollection, Captain Patrick Rechner.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is that information that you received from the security chief of Mr. Milosevic, was that the only information you had directly received about your release and who was involved in your release?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: My question was going to be whether you had received any information from your Bosnian Serb captors regarding your release and who was arranging the release?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, we were told that we were going to be handed over to the Yugoslav security troops, to the Yugoslavian forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, during this time in the buses outside the Presidency, were you able to observe any interaction between the forces that had come from Serbia and the Bosnian Serb forces, those who had been involved in your capture?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: In what way do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you observe who it was who appeared it to be in charge?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I presume it was the security chief of Mr. Milosevic, but, I mean, I did not observe -- I mean, I didn't observe anybody specifically being in charge. At the moment -- at that moment, I was more, well, let's say, happy by our coming release and, to be quite honest, completely fed up with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you able to observe anybody in a co-ordinating role giving out instructions or who was -- who was running things?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to us the witness has already answered this question. That was the previous question that was put to him, whether anybody had been involved in co-ordination and so on. It's already been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that the previous question was more about -- let me just read it again. Yes, Ms. Marcus, if someone doesn't notice any interaction, would you expect him to notice any co-ordination. Co-ordination without interaction is difficult for me to understand, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question and let's --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As far as I understood he said that he didn't observe anyone specifically being in charge but he didn't say whether he observed anybody in a co-ordinating role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, between the -- there was about co-ordination between the -- "Were you able to observe any interaction between the forces that come from Serbia and the Bosnian Serb forces, those who had been involved in your capture?" That is, of course, those who come -- who had arrived for the purposes of the release and the others. But one question more on this matter and then depending on the answer we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question, Mr. Helgers?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not really. For me, the one mostly in charge, as per my recollection, through the whole release process was Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic, so that's who I saw was being in charge at our handing over, and later on, I mean, probably it should have been Mr. Koljevic, but, I mean, I didn't observe any real interaction. It was not clear who was in charge. It was not something that was clearly distinguishable from the bus at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you would like to take a break at this point, I have a few more questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could I inquire, will there be any further examination, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: At this stage, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, we have a good habit to take a -- because you would need five to ten minutes, I take it, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Let me say maximum 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Maximum 15. Then it's certainly useful to take a break now. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, are you ready? Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, at any time during the whole release process, did you see anyone giving instructions to the security chief of Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did you observe the security chief giving instructions to anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: My only recollection of the security chief of Mr. Milosevic is as he was in the bus and made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Now, as the convoy was departing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a technical problem. What I'm saying now is not recorded, nor on video, nor audio. If you look at your screen, you'll see nothing. There is a technical problem. Once it has been identified, I would like to know whether there's a chance that it could be fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have to interrupt this hearing and everyone is requested to remain standby. We have no idea yet how much time it will take to identify the problem and to fix the problem. I'm not a technician, Mr. Helgers, otherwise I would commit myself to -- no, no, it's very unfortunate. I hope that it will not take too much time, especially where we thought ... We would expect easily to finish this afternoon. I still hope that we can. Mr. Jordash, any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, nothing. I was just taking instructions and was caught.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll take another break and we'll see when we can proceed. We stand adjourned. --- Break taken at 4.09 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before I invite you to continue, Ms. Marcus, Mr. Helgers, if at any moment you do not feel well, please, address me and don't hesitate to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus, if you are ready, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Can I find out whether I need to re-ask the questions that I asked after the break or were they recorded or perhaps we would read it back into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. I need the advice of --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I see that the transcript is okay. I'm just wondering about the recording.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the transcript is okay. The only thing then, video is there as well? Video isn't there, transcript is there. If any of the parties would have any problem in proceeding despite the fact that it was only one question, isn't it? The only thing you asked the witness, Ms. Marcus, is whether during the whole of the release process did you see anyone giving instructions to the security chief of Mr. Milosevic. The answer was no. And then: "Did you observe the security chief giving instructions to anybody else." And then he said: "My only recollection of the security chief of Mr. Milosevic is as he was in the bus and made a statement." Does any party insist on having this all said again because there's no video? Then we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, when you departed from -- from Pale, from the Presidency, on the road now to Novi Sad, did you observe any sign of final clearance from the Bosnian Serbs as the convoy drove away, or did you view any signal that the convoy could leave, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not really. The whole trip was, I think we had the road for ourselves. Everything was closed, all the exits and all the roads were blocked so we had one straight trip to -- to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the convoy was escorted by a combined force from Serbia and Bosnian Serbs or --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I saw several civilian -- we were escorted by several civilian police cars and several, well, military, military police cars in which I think they were the Yugoslav security force were in those military cars. They were green.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you able to observe who was in the civilian police military cars?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Civilian cars, to me they looked like civilian Bosnian Serb police cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: During the trip you said you had a clear passage through, so there was no ambush or intercept of the convoy whatsoever along the road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was there any sign of violence of any kind along the way?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No. Sorry, in which -- in which way do you mean violence?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were there any incidents that interrupted the passage?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I do remember passing some sort of Bosnian Serb military unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: What do you recall about that?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: At a certain section there were some military vehicles including armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you stopped at that location?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No, we weren't.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And were you able to observe the demeanour of the Bosnian Serbs at that location as you passed by?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, they were stopped, so we -- I didn't -- we had more or less uninterrupted flow so we could go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did they exchange any salutes or interaction with the passing convoy?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not that I noticed. That's obviously not very easy to see in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Were you stopped --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please move on, Ms. Marcus, before we go to whether they had black or brown tires on their cars, let's -- we're entering detail at this moment. It's cross-examination of a witness who was called for, I think, a rather specific purpose. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, do you recall crossing the border between Bosnia and Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, because it was at a bridge, I don't exactly recollect the location, and there was another media moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Was the media moment before crossing the border or after crossing the border, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I think it was before.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And do you recall observing any interaction between the Bosnian Serbs at that location and the Serbian forces who were escorting you?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Not specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: These are my last questions. Can you comment at all for us on the atmosphere surrounding the release? Sometimes when you think of a hostage release, it can be quite a violent or tense atmosphere, I'm trying to get your -- in your own words, how would you describe the atmosphere surrounding the entire release operation?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's a tough one. Of course it's my interpretation. I'd say it was relaxed. Relatively. I mean, I was a little bit not so relaxed because I was very happy to be released and I had some negative contact with the Bosnian Serbs just prior to the release, but it was quite -- I had the impression it was quite relaxed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Did it appear to you to be very organised?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: It was organised definitely. I would say it was orchestrated because the media moments were, in my impression they were very carefully chosen, the locations, the times.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Helgers, for answering all my questions. Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness. I do have two bar table submissions if you'd like to me make that submission now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps we can deal with them right away. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution seeks to tender into the evidence from the bar table 65 ter 6307.1 and 65 ter 6318. These are videos with corresponding transcripts which contain the portions of the suspect interviews of Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Simatovic which deal with the UN hostages. Let me note before I make my submission on this, that 65 ter 6307.1 is a portion of Prosecution 65 ter 606. That's Mr. Stanisic's suspect interview. And 65 ter 6318 is a portion of Prosecution 65 ter 607, that's Mr. Simatovic's suspect interview. The portion from the accused Stanisic's interview is eight pages of transcript, from the interview date 13 November 2001 and the portion from the accused Simatovic's interview is five pages of transcript from the interview dated 5 February 2002. The B/C/S transcripts of the complete suspect interviews for both accused were disclosed in July 2004 and the English translations in April 2007. The Prosecution submit that this is directly contextualised by this witness the previous witness, DST-036. The Defence has put forth the case that Mr. Stanisic undertook efforts to release the hostages of his own volition and due to his humanitarian concern for their release. They do so --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, I'm just wondering if -- I'd like to ask the witness a few questions in re-examination. I'm wondering if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could not expect, as a matter of fact to that these explanations would follow, but, Ms. Marcus, I think that since you are elaborating on the specific reasons and explaining what the various cases are, that perhaps you deal with it until after we have concluded the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems to be a good suggestion. First of all, any further -- well, I couldn't say further questions. Any questions, Mr. Petrovic, triggered by the cross-examination by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, do you have any further question, yes, apparently you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just a few if I may, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were asked by -- sorry to interrupt you?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: You were asked by my learned friend for the Prosecution about whether the security forces from Yugoslavia, sorry, from Serbia, the ones wearing the red berets, were armed and you said I think they were armed, I probably would have noted if they hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why do you think you would have noted if they hadn't been?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Because, well, that would have stood out because normally you would expect them to be armed. I would expect them to the armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Why in that environment would you expect them be armed?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: The impression I had they were some sort of well, Special Police like force. I do recall later on in Novi Sad, I definitely remember them being armed, but in the previous -- but in Bosnia, I think I would have remembered if they had not been armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could we please have D00474 MFI.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Would you just have a look at this document --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not to be shown to the public, therefore.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This is a document from the General Staff of the VRS, and it's dated, as you can see, four days after your detention?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't see anything because I was -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's coming. Would you just have a look and I want to ask you if you are aware of any of these combat operations on-going in Bosnia at the time of your detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me go to the next page, I want you to read it this. It's a three-page document, I think. Yes. And the last page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could please all unnecessary microphones be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Do these descriptions accord with your understanding of the type of combat operations still on-going in May and June in Gorazde, Sarajevo, and other parts of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Yes, I was at that moment held hostage at the radar station, I can't really say I was able to really follow the operations on the ground so I can't really comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Are you able to comment on whether it was your understanding that there were still active combat of some description in the areas where you were detained or where you travelled through on the way to safety in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Are you aware of active combat in late May, June between French UNPROFOR and the VRS in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: During the time I was held hostage, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, you are not --

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Before that or after that did you become aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, I think there was introduced a multinational brigade which partly consisted of French too, they did some operations, but I think that's outside of this scope.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, you mean it's outside of which scope?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: I mean, it's a considerable time later, I think. At least during the time I was held hostage, I'm not aware of any combat operations. There may well have been, probably there have been, but I was held hostage, I was not really being informed very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm talking about what you learned perhaps later on?

utterances.speaker: MARCUS MARTINUS EMANUEL HELGERS
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Okay. I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: May I tender this from the bar table though, please. Perhaps I can deal with that later with the other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's a bit of an odd document because it tells us what someone intends to do on the 2nd of May, but the document itself is dated the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First page, there's reference to the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't see the 2nd of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll help you out, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Oh, I do see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a bit of a surprise in a document which is dated the 30th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we'll check the original and see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The original also says the 2nd of May, Mr. Jordash, so that doesn't bring you the solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps it's an error in that reference to the 2nd of June is meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Or maybe "for" as it should have said "from". We'll check that and get back to you on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I think if I can just add the English translation of this document does fall quite short of a good English translation, I must say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
