utterances.text: Okay. But the -- from the translation, we see that it's only provisional draft translation that I think decisions on admission can be taken even if there would be an order to have a better translation, but we'll deal with that in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Helgers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Helgers, I have two short questions, when this document was signed by the man you said had a red beret, was this man companied by men similarly dressed or do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several of the Yugoslav security forces present at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they were dressed in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, uniforms, Yugoslav uniforms and red berets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now another question, were you ever involved in how you would be released and to where you would be released, because you find you were released and then taken to Serbia, but to your knowledge has it ever been considered that you would go back to those people who you were working with before you were, that is, to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the Bosnian Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, or at least to the -- to be given over to the UNMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was never informed of any plans that way whatsoever. I mean, we weren't really, I at least wasn't really informed about the whole procedure. It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was a surprise for you, where you were taken, more or less.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was clear we were going to be released because we were all collected and most of the colleagues had already been released, but the exact way in which it was to happen was not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Have my questions triggered any need for further questions, Ms. Marcus, do you have any?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Helgers, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and for having answered all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The following exhibits are not on the 65 ter list and we are requesting permission to add and the Prosecution have no objection to them being added and tendered: 1D05173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, let me see whether we can follow it. 5173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is the map of hostage locations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, part of the 92 ter associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the OTP position was no objection if confirmed by the witness through 92 ter confirmation process. I think it is in his statement that he pointed at that map, so that's confirmed. Yes, next one, Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 74. Any way to identify it on the ...?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's number 37, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 37. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was looking down from 173 down for 174, but I had to look up. Yes, that's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05263, which is again a video of a hostage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, where the name of Mr. Raamakers is spelled. No objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No objection. And 1D05264, which is a VRS intelligence report dated the 26th of May, 1995, no objection. And all these exhibits I've just mentioned are public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D5173 would receive number D514. Document 1D5174, number D515. And document 1D5263 number D516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then 5264 is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D514 up to and including D517 are admitted into evidence. Any more, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The following are documents which were used in the process of examining this witness and we would like to tender the following: 1D05161. Prosecution have no objection if that's bar tabled. It wasn't on the 65 ter list so we apply to add and we apply to bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see what is 5161. It's nowhere on this list?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's number 34, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number 34. And that will receive, Madam Registrar, number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it's admitted into evidence. Next, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05270. It's not on our 65 ter list. The Prosecution have no objection to it being added and tendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to make an amendment to that, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 5270. Is it on the list, on the chart anywhere?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think this was on the chart. I think there was an e-mail exchange before court. However, upon closer examination, the segment of the video -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a video segment, I do understand. Yes, what is the video about, I mean, if we want, is that the part played?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The part played with the two detained hostages on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And number on the chart number 41 is a more complete segment of the same footage and it's quite, I think, quite important in this case to show the previous part, what happened just before those hostages were interviewed, in particular because they're coached as to what to say. So since it's a subset of number 41, that is 1D5153, it appears that the larger segment, with the part where they're coached before provides the most accurate picture of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you would say that gives further context to -- Mr. Jordash, Ms. Marcus is not objecting against admission but wants, for context, to have a broader document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't think they are at the same video, in facts. They are two different ERNs, so I think what my learned friend is asking for is to be added to the exhibit or the proposed exhibit is not in fact part of the same video, but in relation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about trying to agree on whether it is or not, Ms. Marcus, wouldn't that be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I say this though, we can agree on this, that we don't rely upon the truth of what those hostages said. We are not suggesting that what they said was the truth, and we are happy to concede they've been coached for publicity purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I recognise it's not an issue, I mean, I recognise that. At the same time I feel that the context should be there. We can check it and then we can perhaps MFI it for the moment and double-check that this is, actually, a more complete version of that footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What about the following: If it is the same video, then, Mr. Jordash, since you do not dispute that they were coached, then may I take it there is no major objections against that for contextualisation be admitted as well. You agree on what is needed for that and if it's not the same video, then we have your statement here in court that you admit that there was coaching, you concede that they were coached.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, that's conceded. I would need to see the earlier part of the video before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you first try to find out whether it's the same video. If so, you agree on how to produce that, how to tender that and if it's not the same video, Ms. Marcus, then at least you have the concession of Mr. Jordash that coaching was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And then, Your Honour, we would probably seek leave to tender the former portion for context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wanted to keep matters simple. You consider, you discuss the matter and you'll come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We start reserving a number for a video of two persons chained to a bridge either with what happened before, what happened previously, or tendering of two documents. We'll hear from you. The number reserved for one video to start with, Ms. Madam Registrar, would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This would be D519, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D519 is reserved for those purposes. Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: 1D05254. It's not on our 65 ter list. There's no objection to add it -- adding it and there's no objection to tendering it. Apparently earlier on I referred to it and it was recorded on the transcript as 1D05250, which is an error. It's 1D05254 which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Video footage of Jovica Stanisic speaking to released UN hostages. Is that what you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the one. Leave is granted to add it to your 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then it is admitted into evidence under number, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D520, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: And then finally, the last two issues. 1D05265, is also an associated exhibit, I should have dealt with that in the first list. There's no -- it's not on our 65 ter list, there's no objection from the Prosecution to add it and thereafter tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find it -- yes, I see it on the chart under number 41. VRS intelligence and security sector, intelligence regarding UN forces dated the 27th of May. Leave is granted to add it to your 65 ter list and the document is exhibited into evidence under, Madam Registrar, number ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D521, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Thank you. Then finally, D512 was discussed earlier and the Prosecution thought that this was subject to Rule 70 restrictions but it's not. It was a public exhibit in the Karadzic trial, Exhibit P2177.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Rule 70 material is in itself not related to public or not, but of course it would be a bit odd if you would admit publicly into evidence a document and then say, in another case, it should not be used in evidence. That's -- Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: No, I agree, Your Honour. I had checked it but I hadn't found it in the Karadzic case. So if it's admitted publicly, it can be admitted publicly here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution should we not verify that it's admitted publicly.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's admitted publicly, Your Honour, in Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, D512 therefore is now a public document, and we had decided on admission not -- it was marked for identification, or we have admitted already? I think there was -- the issue was whether there was any clearance for this case and I really do not see, even if it has once been Rule 70 material, I can't see any logic in admitting it publicly in one case and even if no clearance is given for another case to not admit it in that other case. Was it Rule 70 material, that's, of course, the first question.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it was originally Rule 70 material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you give the green light and some Rule 70 providers do that specifically for one case, but if it then is a public exhibit, then of course it's totally unimaginable, different from a confidential exhibit, that the same would not apply in any other case.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't understand Your Honours question but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to explain. What does Rule 70 mean? That is to provide material for the purpose of generating further evidence but that information not to be used as evidence. Now, I think there is some practice that some of the Rule 70 providers have given the green light to use a certain document or certain information as evidence, and at the same time say we give this green light only for this particular case. Now, that works only, I would say, if it is admitted confidentially in that case, then there's a way that -- at least there's a possibility of keeping it out of other cases. If it's publicly admitted, I do not see how this is possibly -- could be possibly effective.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour, completely, so since it's been admitted publicly in Karadzic which I hadn't been able to find before, I would say that the Rule 70 restrictions wouldn't apply anymore and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Therefore, D512 is admitted into evidence as a public document. Anything else, Mr. Jordash?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see, D512. What was it exactly? It was the -- could you remind me, Mr. Jordash, what exactly the D512 was? Let me check.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: It's a summary of a news report about the air-strikes. It was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I now remember. It was the document in which all the press reports were represented, and then some comments. If that's all for you, Mr. Petrovic, you've got nothing to ask as far as you are concerned. I take it if you don't jump up, then I take it there are no objections of whatever kind. Ms. Marcus started to explain to us why she considered it reasonable to bar table a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, yes. Our position with respect to these isolated portions of the suspect interviews is that this evidence directly rebuts the Defence position as to the motivation for the accused's involvement in the hostage release. The Prosecution submits that the words of the accused in their own suspect interviews directly rebut the assertions. The suspect interviews show, firstly, that the accused Stanisic did not undertake involvement in the release of the hostages of his own volition but was instructed to do so. And that the motivation for the release was purely political and for the benefit of both the Republika Srpska and Serbia. The accused should not be permitted, in our submission, to benefit from a presumption which neither he nor his co-accused, who was also present at the hostage release, put forward in their own suspect interviews. Therefore, Your Honours, the Prosecution has uploaded, with the 65 ter number 6307.1 and 6318, the videos of those interviews with the corresponding transcripts, and tenders them from the bar table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, there are objections to that application. Firstly, there's been no proper notice that this would form part of the Prosecution case. They've had notice of the accused's position in relation to the hostages for well on seven years and yet have failed to issue any notice whatsoever that these would form part of their case. Number one. Number two, that obviously has certain consequences. It has consequences in terms of fundamental right to be informed of the nature and cause of the Prosecution case. To suddenly add to the Prosecution case this at the end or towards the end of the first accused Defence case, cannot in our submission reasonably be considered to be proper notice and is of course, in our submission, a complete violation of the accused's right to know the case against him. Secondly, I'm not sure that I understand the Prosecution's reasons for using this interview. I haven't had time to look properly at the interviews because we were ambushed by this application at the last minute. No notice came forward at a time we could have adequately prepared for the submission, so I'm doing it off the top of my head, as I think of the issues arising. It would have been good and useful to have proper notice of the argument. But in relation to what my learned friend says are the reasons, I don't think Mr. Stanisic has ever said that he took action to negotiate the release of the hostages of his own volition. It would be an absurd position to advance, that he picked himself up from Belgrade and headed out to save the hostages without any instruction or order from any other senior or leader, or senior authority. Where my learned friend gets that from is a mystery to me. In relation to the second point that it was not for the benefit or that Mr. Stanisic, as I understand it, has somehow misled the Court by claiming that it was for a different purpose, I don't think we've ever in the Defence excluded any particular reason. We say in our Defence that the reason he, Stanisic, acted as he did was for a number of reasons. One, because he had been instructed to do so. Two, because he had concern for the hostages. And, three, because the hostage crisis was undermining and preventing the Contact Group from continuing to negotiate peace. There's a number of reasons, and in our submission, that's obvious. My learned friends's submissions, in our submission, are not specific enough to justify such a violation, if it can be justified, of the accused's right to be informed of the case. My learned friend should, at the very minimum, in our submission, take us to the portions of those interviews which she says somehow rebuts a position which we have put forward which cannot sustained on the basis of these interviews. Because without that we are floating in the dark. Those are our submissions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we also object to the admission of these segments of an interview and we support what my learned friend Mr. Jordash said. We would also add that, considering that this is something very specific as an interview with the accused, we wish to be granted some time from you so that considering the specific legal practice in this court we might state our position about this in a motion that we would file. And I would also use this opportunity to say that when Mr. Simatovic gave this interview, he had not been freed from his obligation to keep state secrets, which throws a specific light on the contents of what he said in that interview. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just to respond briefly. The complete suspect interviews were on the 65 ter list from the beginning. The Prosecution, in the end, did not seek to tender them because generally we find the interviews to be entirely self-serving. In this particular instance, the fact that a self-serving interview should not contain any assertion that the release of the hostages was, as Mr. Jordash said, because he had concern for the hostages, demonstrates that this is something that was created by the Defence later. It directly rebuts one thing that Mr. Jordash just said and what they've put forward which they seek to use in mitigation and they seek to use to impact upon the intent that's found by the Chamber with respect to the commission of crimes. These portions of the suspect interviews, very brief portions, eight pages for Mr. Stanisic and five for Mr. Simatovic, are focused specifically on the UN hostage issue. They are isolated and only on that issue. Those are the only portions we seek to tender and there is no mention by either accused of any concern for the hostages as any part of any of the discussion relating to the hostages. Therefore, Your Honours, we feel that it is in fact directly related to what evidence the Defence has led in this respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Just very briefly if I may, two things. It doesn't matter, in our submission, that the Prosecution discloses these documents to us at a given time. They've disclosed hundreds of thousands of documents to or pages of documents over the last seven or eight years. We can't be expected to just make a blanket assumption that they are going to be part of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, you are talking about disclosure, Ms. Marcus is talking about having it on the 65 ter list. That's not exactly the same, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, it is the same to us in the sense that if it's not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you put a document on the 65 ter list when you seriously consider to use that as evidence and that is not, I would say that's for electronic disclosure under Rule 68(ii) it is not -- that's disclosure, but if it's not on the 65 ter list, there's even a fair expectation that the party disclosing it doesn't intend to seek it to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just linguistically trying to understand, you are using words which are not the same as the ones used by Ms. Marcus. I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- clarify it first. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I accept that there is a distinction. I cannot recall actually Mr. Stanisic's interview being on the 65 ter list. It was something that I thought was rather curious at the time. I might have got that wrong, but, again, we haven't had a chance to check this because we've been ambushed by the argument. But I would ask that we be given some time, just a little time just to check whether that's correct because I don't think it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Petrovic asked for more time, you asked for more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I'm not going to cut you off in your argument, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I do accept there is a distinction, but it's -- in the end it's a distinction without a difference when a document is produced from the non-65 ter disclosure or the 65 ter list at this late stage. The issue of prejudice is the same. We cannot be expected to guess at what documents might come into the case at the end of the first accused's defence or towards the end. We ought to have proper notice that it will form part of the Prosecution case. That's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask you one question: Why exactly -- why exactly did you call this witness? To establish what?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: To establish what happened during the meeting with Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any dispute about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think that it seems almost everything is disputed by the Prosecution in relation to the Defence case, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, that's not an answer to my question, is it? Of course to say I call whatever witnesses because I cannot -- was there dispute about what happened during this very short moment when the witness met Mr. Stanisic very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I don't know is the answer to that because I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would have been good to try to find that out because if that's the purpose of calling a witness from far away, that's -- I would have checked, first of all, whether there's any dispute about that. Okay. That's what you wanted to establish what was said -- it was 92 ter, not 92 bis because the testimony was there, the statement was there. And that's, of course, the moment to consider whether it's in dispute yes or no. If it's not in dispute, then 92 bis is easier, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, we took the view, sorry, Your Honour, we took the view given that the Prosecution have objected to every 92 bis application we've made and we anticipated they would, that we better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not true, Mr. Jordash. Isn't it? DST-070.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I said almost every.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think you said to every 92 bis application we've made, that's what the transcript says and that's what I heard you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Sorry, I thought I said almost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But apart from one, I think, they've objected. On a basis which is much less, we would submit, than the issue of the witness testifying to the acts and conduct of the accused. This witness was going to testify in our view, to the acts and conduct of the accused and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that may have been a good reason to call him, I admit that, that it's directly acts and conduct of the accused. I stand corrected in that respect. Yes, and you would say that nothing in the evidence is such that the motives were part of what you sought to establish?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Absolutely -- well. Well, I think in some way we were going to motive because we were saying that Mr. Stanisic had behaved properly and in a way which perhaps the Bosnian Serbs had not, certainly in the way that the Bosnian Serbs had not, so we were saying that his behaviour was proper and reasonable and reassuring. So we were in that sense going to how Mr. Stanisic had behaved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And in your questioning you have asked some attention for at least for that it is not a nice situation to be in if you were a hostage, so, therefore, I would say the humanitarian aspect comes up there although not perhaps very explicit, but it allows you to argue that --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Therefore, of course I'm thinking about how fair or unfair it is, whether to what extent the hostage issue was part of the Prosecution's case or whether the Prosecution is rebutting something which, perhaps, implicitly is there. I think we have to -- I have to discuss it -- we have to, the Chamber has to discuss it anyway. You are asking for more time. Anything you would like to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Only one thing, the premise of the Prosecution's submission is also not correct. If one looks at paragraph -- sorry, page 34 of this transcript of Mr. Stanisic's interview, he emphasises, nobody was hurt, I made sure that the officers who were without uniforms and without weapons that they looked dignified and they not be humiliated, I think this was done very directly. So there is evidence in this interview of his humanitarian concern and perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that is, I would say that's -- I think whenever one party selects a certain portion of a document, the other party is always given an opportunity to further contextualise that and if you say, well, it sheds light on the fact that there may have been various motives and that the political one doesn't necessarily exclude. I would say politicians are not per definition ignoring humanitarian grounds, I mean, that's -- any suggestion in that direction might cause some problems in the political world. I'm not in the political world. If you want to add that -- this for context, would you have any objection to that, Ms. Marcus?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: That's part of the exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of the exhibit, but is it also part of the pages you have selected.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, it is not our position that the adding of context is permissible in all instances. What overrides that is the fundamental right be informed of the nature and cause of the charges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your basic objection is there. Only I was wondering that if, and I can't anticipate what the Chamber will decide, but if it would admit it, whether there would be any other portions you would like to add for contextualisation, and it was purely theoretical at this moment because we have to consider, after we've heard from you further, whether or not we'll admit the two -- the portions of the interviews the Prosecution is tendering. Any other argument to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Well, I would only add this: If Your Honours -- I mean, given Your Honours' approach to the admission of evidence, we would expect this document to come in now and I would then request that this document come in for the very specific reason which has been put forward, that it displays, according to the Prosecution, a lack of motive for, shall we say, humanitarian concerns and not for any other reason, because I look through this interview and I see other aspects which I'm absolutely sure the Prosecution will want to rely upon as the truth of the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is to some extent new, Mr. Jordash. Usually we've said you can add something for contextualisation. If you say there's context in it which is inappropriate to be presented so cut it down, that would be a new approach but we would have to consider that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: This portion of the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, any other argument? You say I'm concerned about portions in there not dealing with the matter for which Ms. Marcus tenders the document and you would like to have that taken out if the Chamber would decide to admit that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, and I would like the Prosecution to be restricted to the use of this portion if they are allowed to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, that is a clear position. Ms. Marcus, any further comments on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Only, Your Honour, that this is the portion that deals with the UN hostages. For the context of what the accused is saying, I think it would be taken out of context to take a portion out of it. Otherwise, I've made my submissions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what you are exclusively aiming to establish that. Yes. Let me just consult my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash, the Chamber will further consider the matter which also allows you to take a bit more time. When do you think you could make further submissions, it's perhaps not a matter for which we'd need written submissions, I think it can be dealt with orally and the Chamber will then better be able to decide on admission, yes or no, and then the next step would be if we consider to admit it, that you then say, but please take this out, please take that out. Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The problem we have is that it's plain to us that the Prosecution intends to use this document for the wider purposes and that's why my learned friend insists that the whole document should go in. I think the fair approach is for the Prosecution to lay out their position in totality as to why they want this document so that we can deal with everything at one point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the whole document, we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The whole excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is your concern, then why not sit together and say our concern is mainly focusing on this portion and then Ms. Marcus could consider whether or not that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: But our concern is the -- sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, you are objecting. We give you further time to consider it. We say we will not decide at this very moment. You make further submissions. But then it was silent for five seconds and then you said, well, we think that the Prosecution is tendering for other purposes and why not try to see whether that's true or not. Ms. Marcus apparently says that that's not her purpose. If you can agree on any such matter, please present it to the Chamber. If not, we'll hear your further arguments and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If the Prosecution are not prepared to stand up now and say they will not use this document for any other purpose than that which they've indicated, then I don't think us sitting down with the Prosecution is going to assist, if they won't do it in open court, they won't do it behind the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The Prosecution intends, would intend, to use this document for the purpose of rebutting the Defence case as to the -- the involvement of Mr. Stanisic in the release of the hostages. So the arguments that the Defence puts forward as to mitigation or the impact on mens rea of the accused as they will derive from his involvement in the release of the UN hostages, the Prosecution will put this forward as one piece of the evidence to rebut that assertion and for that purpose only.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: In other words, they can use any part of the document for any purpose whatsoever. That's what that amounts to. If it's mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's for that purpose only, yes, mens rea not actus reus.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: If it's mens rea they can pick out anything from this transcript and say this shows Stanisic's mens rea in relation to the charges. There's nothing specific about what my learned friend has said to limit them in any way to the use of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me read.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As to mitigation or the impact on the mens rea of the accused. It's not only mitigation, it's also impact, Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: It's to rebut the Defence's case that the viva voce in the UN hostage release should serve as mitigation or should impact somehow on the mens rea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Somehow, that apparently is --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Well, it's unclear -- the Defence has made broad representations about the fact that this involvement will -- will in some way demonstrate that the accused didn't have the mens rea for the commission of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence gets more time to make further submissions. The Chamber will then decide on admission, yes or no, and we'll hear further submissions if need be for widening or broadening or limiting the selected portions. At the same time, I would urge the parties to see whether they can agree on this matter in one way or another and to find such a formulation that we don't have to spend on this for ages where I would say the main purpose for the Prosecution and the main concern by the Defence are clear, and I wonder whether with good intentions from both sides there's any way to reconcile the two positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I, Your Honour, yes, I just for Your Honours' information, it was on the 65 ter list until the 16th of May, 2008, when it was dropped from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I will double-check that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If that's the case, I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then this may be part of your further submissions. Any other matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we expect the submission to be oral I'll not set a dead-line but at the earliest convenient moment you should be prepared to make such submissions. Then, practically, we have no further witness for this week?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: No, we've contacted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we are uncertain about even next week, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We spoke to the witness DST-060 last week when the application had been made. He was aware of it, he is aware it's -- I think we spoke to him actually after the decision had been made, and he is aware of it and it's coming -- he is aware it's coming and he is aware it's demanding what it's demanding. And we contacted the Registry this morning and there was no news, so we are in the dark really as is, I think, everyone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, which means that, of course, we hope to hear the evidence of Witness DST-060 before we start with the Defence case, the Simatovic Defence case, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But can't say much about it at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you allow me just a minute. [French on English channel] [Overlapping speakers] ... on the cross-examination of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I love the French language but I got it on my English channel. I think -- could you please restart, Mr. Bakrac, I allow you a minute, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I'll try to restrict myself to just one minute. Could the Trial Chamber please render a decision on the cross-examination of Witness Manojlo Milovanovic, we believe that his cross-examination and further questioning would affect our own Defence case and the possibility of calling certain witness and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only thing I can say that we are working hard on the decision and sometimes even before the decision is in every respect finalised that we would perhaps even inform you already. But we'll see how that develops, but it's -- we'll deal with it with priority. Any other matter? Which means that we will adjourn, there being no witnesses this week, we'll adjourn until Monday, the 21st of November, 3.00 in the afternoon for the 54 bis hearing. And isn't it true that there were some -- I heard -- I was informed that there was a problem with the scheduling of that hearing, from what I understand, not from the parties?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: From our side, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. But --

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Nothing from our side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I know that, but the problem, if it is there, it comes from ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is a document which was just handed out to me. Just read the title, it has not been filed: "The Republic of Serbia's notice of objection in relation to the Trial Chamber I order from the 4th of November, 2011 scheduling a hearing." So apparently there is something, I haven't read it yet, it's ten pages approximately. So let's first read it. Therefore, perhaps it's wiser to adjourn sine die but you it could be the 21st of November, it could be the 22nd of November, it could be the 23rd, we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Could I query one thing. Do Your Honours envisage that the hearing will involve, or should involve, the examination of the relevant official? I ask because I'd like the opportunity to prepare to conduct that examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What do you mean exactly by examination? I think we invited but I'm now talking by top of my head, we invited the Republic of Serbia to appear so that we had an opportunity to discuss with them or at least ask questions about -- whether you call that an examination, certainly not like a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I'm trying to see the distinction between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, yes, you can ask questions to a state and of course, it's a physical person who has to appear and give the answers, but for example, a witness takes the oath. That's not the position, as I understand it, at this moment, the position of representatives and by the Republic of Serbia to attend the hearing. Of course, we expect answers to any questions that there may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Then, I understand the position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any further matter? If not, we stand adjourned sine die. Parties should be prepared for a hearing on the 21st of November if that scheduling stands. Otherwise depending on the appearance of witness during that week for the days after that.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.29 p.m.,
